screens.title: Workspace vs Configuration Space
screens.narratorSegment: Workspace and configuration space are two complementary ways to think about robot motion. The workspace is the physical 3D volume where the robot’s end-effector can be placed — for a six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, imagine a reachable volume bounded by link lengths and joint limits. The configuration space, or C-space, is the set of all joint-angle combinations; for a 6-DOF arm the C-space is six-dimensional. This matters because obstacles that are simple in workspace become complex shapes — C-obstacles — in configuration space. Planning algorithms operate in C-space so they can reason about collisions with the whole robot body, not just the end-effector. A concrete example: moving an arm around a table. In workspace you see a forbidden region the end-effector must avoid; in C-space that maps to curved forbidden regions that block some joint-angle paths but not others. A common misconception is to plan only in workspace for manipulators; that can miss collisions where a link sweeps through an obstacle even when the end-effector path looks clear. Key takeaway: map workspace obstacles into C-space and plan there so collision constraints become explicit constraints on joint variables. How will you visualize high-dimensional C-space when designing planners for multi-DOF manipulators?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Workspace vs C-space
Definition

Workspace and Configuration Space

Two representations: physical positions the robot can reach, versus the set of joint angles that parameterize its pose.

Concrete example

For a 6-DOF arm, workspace is a 3D volume of reachable end-effector poses; C-space is 6-dimensional, one axis per joint angle.

Misconception

Planning only in workspace may miss link collisions. Always check full body motion by mapping to C-space.

Key Takeaway

Plan in C-space for correctness; use workspace for intuitive visualization and goal specification.

Visual comparison
Workspace

3D positions and orientations the end-effector can reach; obstacles appear as forbidden volumes.

Configuration Space

High-dimensional joint-angle space where collision constraints become C-obstacles for planner search.

Why it matters

Planners that search C-space correctly capture self-collisions and swept-volume constraints; workspace-only planners risk unsafe motions.

screens.title: The Kalman Filter: Prediction and Update
screens.narratorSegment: The Kalman Filter proceeds in two alternating steps: prediction and update. In the prediction step we use the system model — the state transition matrix and control input — to propagate the mean state and its uncertainty forward in time. The covariance prediction projects uncertainty through the dynamics and adds process noise. The correct covariance formula is essential: P goes to A P A prime plus Q, not A P plus Q. A common coding bug is to omit the right-hand A transpose, which yields incorrect uncertainty growth. In the update step we incorporate a measurement: compute the Kalman gain, compare the measurement to the predicted measurement (the innovation), and correct the state and covariance. Practically, the Kalman gain balances trust between prediction and measurement based on their covariances. A concrete example: a 1D position-velocity system where position is predicted from velocity. If you implement the prediction without A' the filter will underestimate or misorient uncertainty and the gain will mis-weight sensor evidence. Misconception check: the Kalman Filter is optimal only for linear dynamics and Gaussian noise. When the system is nonlinear the EKF approximates this by linearization, but that introduces approximation error. Takeaway: implement both state and covariance predictions carefully and always test with known noise levels to confirm the covariance evolves as expected.

keyIdea.title: Essential Formula
keyIdea.text: Prediction: x = A x + B u; P = A P A' + Q. Update: compute Kalman gain, correct state with the innovation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Kalman Filter Steps
Process

Prediction & Update

Prediction (state)
x = A x + B u — propagate the mean using the system model and control input.
Prediction (covariance)
P = A P A' + Q — project uncertainty through dynamics and add process noise. Omitting A' is a common bug.
Update
Compute Kalman gain K = P_pred H' (H P_pred H' + R)^{-1}, apply innovation to correct state and covariance.
Key Takeaway

Both state and covariance propagation must be correct. Test with known noise to validate behavior.

Code snippet (covariance bug)
% Incorrect:
P = A * P + Q;

% Correct:
P = A * P * A' + Q;
Run unit tests where A rotates uncertainty to confirm the A' term is present. Without it the covariance will not represent the rotated uncertainty correctly.

screens.title: Kalman, EKF, and Particle Filter — When to Use Which
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an estimator depends on model linearity and the shape of the belief distribution. The Kalman Filter assumes linear dynamics and Gaussian noise, representing the state with a single mean and covariance. The EKF extends this approach to nonlinear systems by linearizing the model around the current estimate; it works well near a correct estimate but can diverge if the linearization point is poor. The particle filter represents arbitrary distributions using a cloud of weighted particles, which makes it well suited for global localization when the initial position is unknown or multimodal. The resampling step in a particle filter redraws particles with replacement proportional to weight, concentrating the particle set on high-probability hypotheses and allowing the filter to converge from a uniform prior. A common misconception is that EKF can handle arbitrary nonlinearity simply by linearizing; in practice, when the belief is multimodal or highly non-Gaussian, the particle filter is the right choice despite higher computational cost. A concrete scenario: a robot dropped randomly in a map should use a particle filter for global localization; an EKF cannot represent the initial uniform or multimodal belief. Takeaway: match estimator assumptions to the problem — unimodal linear systems use Kalman; weakly nonlinear cases with small error use EKF; global or highly nonlinear multimodal problems use particle filters.

keyIdea.text: Kalman = linear Gaussian; EKF = linearized nonlinear; Particle = multimodal, arbitrary distributions with resampling concentrating hypotheses.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Estimator Comparison
Comparison

Kalman vs EKF vs Particle

Kalman Filter
Single Gaussian, linear models, computationally light, optimal under assumptions.
Extended Kalman Filter
Linearizes nonlinear models around the estimate. Works locally; vulnerable to poor initialization.
Particle Filter
Nonparametric belief representation, supports multimodal and global localization. Resampling concentrates hypotheses by weight.
Concrete example

If a robot has no initial pose estimate, initialize particles uniformly across the map and let sensor updates and resampling focus particles near the true pose. The EKF cannot represent that initial uniform uncertainty because it uses a single Gaussian.

Misconception

Believing EKF can handle arbitrary nonlinearity by repeated linearization. EKF is an approximation that fails for multimodal beliefs.

Key Takeaway

Match estimator assumptions to your task: use particle filters for global or multimodal uncertainty, EKF for mild nonlinearity, Kalman for linear Gaussian problems.

screens.title: Potential Field Controller — Behavior and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: The potential field controller forms a virtual force field: an attractive force pulls the robot toward the goal and repulsive forces push it away from obstacles. The provided MATLAB controller computes an attractive term proportional to the distance to the goal and a repulsive term inversely proportional to the cube of distance to obstacles. While intuitive, this design commonly produces local minima where attractive and repulsive forces cancel and trap the robot. The answer key highlights two practical problems: the unlimited influence of obstacles in the code and the local minimum phenomenon. A better design limits obstacle influence to a finite radius d0 so distant obstacles do not affect motion, and adds escape strategies such as random perturbation or path replanning to recover from minima. For example, if the robot is centered between two nearby obstacles and tries to move toward a goal that lies beyond them, the repulsive forces from each side can balance the attractive force and stall the robot. Misconception check: potential fields are not guaranteed to find a path in complex environments; they are simple but fragile. Key takeaway: use potential fields for local reactive behavior but combine them with global planners or minima-escape strategies for reliable navigation.

keyIdea.title: Local Minimum
keyIdea.text: Potential fields can trap robots; limit obstacle influence with distance d0 and add escape rules or global planners.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Potential Fields
Code Analysis

Attractive and Repulsive Forces

function F = controller(q, q_goal, obstacles)
    F = -2 * (q - q_goal);           % attractive
    for i = 1:length(obstacles)
        d = norm(q - obstacles{i});
        F = F + 10 * (q - obstacles{i}) / d^3;  % repulsive
    end
end
The code above lacks a finite influence distance for obstacles and can create singularly large repulsive forces when d is small. The local minimum problem appears when attractive and repulsive vectors cancel. Fixes include limiting repulsion to d < d0 and adding randomness or planning to escape minima.
Practical fixes
  • Use finite influence radius d0 so obstacles beyond d0 do not contribute.
  • Clip repulsive force magnitude to avoid singularities at very small d.
  • Combine with a planner or add escape heuristics for minima.
Warning

Do not rely on potential fields alone for guaranteed navigation in complex maps.

screens.title: Fixing a Kalman Covariance Bug
screens.narratorSegment: A subtle but critical bug in Kalman Filter implementations is incorrect covariance prediction. The exam code example showed P = A * P + Q, which is missing the right multiplication by A transpose. The correct propagation is P = A * P * A' + Q. This term rotates and scales the covariance ellipse according to system dynamics; without it, the covariance loses the correct orientation and size as the state evolves. To test your implementation, use a state transition that rotates the state, such as a constant angular velocity in a 2D pose. Start with a diagonal covariance and observe whether the uncertainty ellipse rotates with the state. If your code lacks A', the ellipse will not rotate and subsequent Kalman gains will be miscomputed, causing either overconfidence or underconfidence in sensor updates. A practical debugging pattern: run a synthetic simulation where A is known and process noise Q is zero; compute the analytic P and compare to the implementation at each step. Misconception check: adding Q does not compensate for the missing A'—it merely inflates uncertainty but does not give it the correct orientation. Key takeaway: always include the full A P A' term and verify with rotation or shear transformations to detect implementation errors.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Covariance Bug
The incorrect code
% Buggy covariance prediction
P = A * P + Q;
Corrected form
% Correct covariance propagation
P = A * P * A' + Q;
Validate with a test where A rotates the state. Compare elements of P step-by-step. Missing A' will break the off-diagonal terms and mislead the Kalman gain computation.
Quick test
  1. Set Q = 0 and choose A as a small rotation matrix.
  2. Initialize P diagonal and step the prediction several times analytically and numerically.
  3. Confirm that P rotates consistent with A in the correct implementation.
Key Takeaway

The A' term preserves covariance orientation. Use simple synthetic tests to reveal its absence.

screens.title: Euler Angles, Rotation Order, and Gimbal Lock
screens.narratorSegment: The provided Euler-to-rotation-matrix code computes Rx, Ry, and Rz and multiplies them as Rx * Ry * Rz. The principal logic error is assuming an implicit rotation convention without documenting the order. Rotation matrices do not commute; the multiplication order determines the actual sequence of rotations and thus the final orientation. The exam answer points out that for the common aerospace Z-Y-X convention (roll-pitch-yaw), the correct composition is R = Rz * Ry * Rx. Another critical issue is gimbal lock: when pitch equals plus or minus ninety degrees, two rotation axes align and the system loses a degree of freedom, producing singular behavior. This is not a code bug per se, but an inherent limitation of Euler angles. The remedy is to switch to quaternion representations for robust orientation handling or to carefully document the rotation convention and guard against singular pitch angles. A concrete example: for theta equal to ninety degrees, Rx and Rz can align making yaw indistinguishable from roll. Misconception check: changing the multiplication order does not merely re-label axes; it fundamentally changes the mapping from Euler parameters to orientation. Key takeaway: always specify rotation order, test edge cases near ±90 degrees, and prefer quaternions when avoiding gimbal lock is required.

keyIdea.title: Rotation Convention
keyIdea.text: Rotation order is essential; Rx*Ry*Rz is not equivalent to Rz*Ry*Rx. Gimbal lock happens at ±90° pitch; quaternions avoid that singularity.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Euler Rotation Pitfalls
Definition & Bug

Order matters — and so does singularity

% Provided code
Rx = [1 0 0; 0 cos(phi) -sin(phi); 0 sin(phi) cos(phi)];
Ry = [cos(theta) 0 sin(theta); 0 1 0; -sin(theta) 0 cos(theta)];
Rz = [cos(psi) -sin(psi) 0; sin(psi) cos(psi) 0; 0 0 1];
R = Rx * Ry * Rz; % ambiguous convention
The correct standard Z-Y-X aerospace order is R = Rz * Ry * Rx. If theta equals ±90 degrees expect gimbal lock. Consider quaternions to avoid singularities when continuous orientation coverage is required.
Practical checks
  • Document rotation convention clearly (intrinsic vs extrinsic).
  • Test edge angles near ±90° to reveal singular behavior.
  • Use quaternions for long sequences of rotations or interpolation.
Why it matters

Orientation bugs are subtle and often manifest only near singular configurations or during interpolation; rigorous tests prevent costly failures on hardware.

screens.title: Camera Intrinsics and Structure from Motion Scale Ambiguity
screens.narratorSegment: Camera intrinsic parameters describe internal camera properties: focal length, principal point, and lens distortion coefficients. These parameters map 3D camera coordinates to pixel coordinates and are essential for accurate projection and triangulation. Bundle adjustment, used in Structure from Motion, refines camera poses and 3D points by minimizing reprojection error across all views; it optimizes poses and point coordinates jointly to produce a maximum likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise assumptions. However, monocular SfM cannot determine absolute scene scale because the essential or fundamental matrix recovers translation only up to a scalar factor. In other words, from a single moving camera you can infer relative geometry but not absolute distances without a scale reference, such as a known object size or stereo baseline. A common practical consequence is that reconstructions from a single camera must be scaled later if metric measurements are required. Misconception check: higher-quality images or better feature matches do not remove the scale ambiguity; only additional metric information or sensors (e. g., stereo baseline, IMU, or known object sizes) resolve scale. Key takeaway: calibrate intrinsics carefully and remember that monocular SfM needs an external scale reference for metric reconstructions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.3 › Camera & SfM
Definition

Intrinsics & Bundle Adjustment

Intrinsics include focal length, principal point, and distortion — they define how camera geometry maps to pixels. Bundle adjustment jointly optimizes camera poses and 3D points to minimize reprojection error.

Purpose of bundle adjustment

Refine all camera parameters and 3D points simultaneously to correct accumulated pose and triangulation errors.

Scale ambiguity

Monocular SfM recovers translation only up to a scale factor because the essential matrix determines direction not magnitude. Without a metric reference, absolute distances are unknown.

Practical fix

Introduce a known baseline, a calibration object, or fuse IMU data to recover metric scale.

screens.narratorSegment: The practical problem presents a two-wheeled mobile inverted pendulum with state [x; x_dot; theta; theta_dot]. The recommended design is a cascade controller: an inner balance loop stabilizes the pendulum angle theta near zero, and an outer position loop commands a small desired tilt to move the robot toward the target position. Concretely, the outer loop computes a desired tilt from position error, which the inner loop then tracks using high-gain feedback on theta and theta_dot. The exam provides tuned gains and a full MATLAB simulation along with an EKF for state estimation. The EKF fuses noisy IMU measurements of theta and theta_dot and noisy encoder measurements of x_dot. Key implementation notes: limit desired tilt to safe bounds, saturate motor commands to prevent unrealistic forces, and set sensible process and measurement covariances in the EKF. A practical misconception is to design position control that assumes perfect balance; instead the outer loop must work through the inner balance loop by commanding tilt. The simulation shows balance at rest for three seconds, then a commanded move to x = 3 m. Takeaway: cascade architectures separate fast stabilization from slower task-level goals and an EKF cleans noisy sensors so controllers operate reliably.

fullNarratorScript:
This final chapter compiles exam questions and authoritative answers across the course’s core topics. You will review how homogeneous transforms combine rotation and translation, why A* gains efficiency with a heuristic, and how filters like the Kalman Filter, EKF, and particle filter differ in their assumptions and use cases. We also revisit practical diagnostics: potential fields and local minima, a common covariance bug in Kalman code, and the ambiguity of Euler rotation conventions. Finally, a full practical problem shows a cascade controller and an Extended Kalman Filter applied to a two-wheeled balancing robot, complete with simulation code. Working through these solutions helps you consolidate where subtle errors commonly appear and how to reason about trade-offs: accuracy versus computation, unimodal versus multimodal state representations, and design choices between wheels and legs for terrain. As you explore the screens, pay attention to the concrete code examples and their fixes, the conceptual contrasts that reveal common misconceptions, and the design rationale behind the balancing robot. Ask yourself which solution patterns you would reuse on your own robot and where you still want more practice.

These learning objectives map directly to the concepts and solutions in the answer key. First, you will be able to explain and use homogeneous transforms to represent rotation and translation together, which is essential when chaining frames in kinematics. Second, you will interpret estimator choices: contrast a Kalman Filter, the EKF, and a particle filter and choose the right estimator for global localization, sensor fusion, or real-time linear systems. Third, you will diagnose common code faults: recognize incorrect covariance propagation, rotation-order mistakes that lead to gimbal lock, and potential-field traps that create local minima. Fourth, you will design a practical control system: compose an inner stabilizing controller and an outer position loop and implement an EKF to fuse noisy IMU and encoder data. Each objective focuses on both conceptual understanding and practical skills so you can reason about trade-offs and implement robust solutions in simulation or on hardware.

These practice objectives translate knowledge into demonstrable tasks. For transforms, construct a chained forward kinematics calculation using homogeneous matrices and show how composition preserves rotation and translation. For estimation, implement the prediction and update steps of a Kalman Filter in code and then extend it to an EKF for a simple nonlinear sensor model. For planning, compare A* with Dijkstra on a small grid and observe how a heuristic reduces explored nodes. For controllers and code diagnostics, reproduce the potential field controller, then add a finite influence distance and an anti-stuck escape rule. Each task is designed to force you to apply the theory to code, and to reflect on typical misconceptions: assuming linearity when the system is nonlinear, treating sensor noise as negligible, or ignoring singularities in rotation representations. Completing these practice tasks verifies not only recall, but also the ability to reason about implementation choices under realistic constraints.

Workspace and configuration space are two complementary ways to think about robot motion. The workspace is the physical 3D volume where the robot’s end-effector can be placed — for a six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, imagine a reachable volume bounded by link lengths and joint limits. The configuration space, or C-space, is the set of all joint-angle combinations; for a 6-DOF arm the C-space is six-dimensional. This matters because obstacles that are simple in workspace become complex shapes — C-obstacles — in configuration space. Planning algorithms operate in C-space so they can reason about collisions with the whole robot body, not just the end-effector. A concrete example: moving an arm around a table. In workspace you see a forbidden region the end-effector must avoid; in C-space that maps to curved forbidden regions that block some joint-angle paths but not others. A common misconception is to plan only in workspace for manipulators; that can miss collisions where a link sweeps through an obstacle even when the end-effector path looks clear. Key takeaway: map workspace obstacles into C-space and plan there so collision constraints become explicit constraints on joint variables. How will you visualize high-dimensional C-space when designing planners for multi-DOF manipulators?

The Kalman Filter proceeds in two alternating steps: prediction and update. In the prediction step we use the system model — the state transition matrix and control input — to propagate the mean state and its uncertainty forward in time. The covariance prediction projects uncertainty through the dynamics and adds process noise. The correct covariance formula is essential: P goes to A P A prime plus Q, not A P plus Q. A common coding bug is to omit the right-hand A transpose, which yields incorrect uncertainty growth. In the update step we incorporate a measurement: compute the Kalman gain, compare the measurement to the predicted measurement (the innovation), and correct the state and covariance. Practically, the Kalman gain balances trust between prediction and measurement based on their covariances. A concrete example: a 1D position-velocity system where position is predicted from velocity. If you implement the prediction without A' the filter will underestimate or misorient uncertainty and the gain will mis-weight sensor evidence. Misconception check: the Kalman Filter is optimal only for linear dynamics and Gaussian noise. When the system is nonlinear the EKF approximates this by linearization, but that introduces approximation error. Takeaway: implement both state and covariance predictions carefully and always test with known noise levels to confirm the covariance evolves as expected.

Choosing an estimator depends on model linearity and the shape of the belief distribution. The Kalman Filter assumes linear dynamics and Gaussian noise, representing the state with a single mean and covariance. The EKF extends this approach to nonlinear systems by linearizing the model around the current estimate; it works well near a correct estimate but can diverge if the linearization point is poor. The particle filter represents arbitrary distributions using a cloud of weighted particles, which makes it well suited for global localization when the initial position is unknown or multimodal. The resampling step in a particle filter redraws particles with replacement proportional to weight, concentrating the particle set on high-probability hypotheses and allowing the filter to converge from a uniform prior. A common misconception is that EKF can handle arbitrary nonlinearity simply by linearizing; in practice, when the belief is multimodal or highly non-Gaussian, the particle filter is the right choice despite higher computational cost. A concrete scenario: a robot dropped randomly in a map should use a particle filter for global localization; an EKF cannot represent the initial uniform or multimodal belief. Takeaway: match estimator assumptions to the problem — unimodal linear systems use Kalman; weakly nonlinear cases with small error use EKF; global or highly nonlinear multimodal problems use particle filters.

The potential field controller forms a virtual force field: an attractive force pulls the robot toward the goal and repulsive forces push it away from obstacles. The provided MATLAB controller computes an attractive term proportional to the distance to the goal and a repulsive term inversely proportional to the cube of distance to obstacles. While intuitive, this design commonly produces local minima where attractive and repulsive forces cancel and trap the robot. The answer key highlights two practical problems: the unlimited influence of obstacles in the code and the local minimum phenomenon. A better design limits obstacle influence to a finite radius d0 so distant obstacles do not affect motion, and adds escape strategies such as random perturbation or path replanning to recover from minima. For example, if the robot is centered between two nearby obstacles and tries to move toward a goal that lies beyond them, the repulsive forces from each side can balance the attractive force and stall the robot. Misconception check: potential fields are not guaranteed to find a path in complex environments; they are simple but fragile. Key takeaway: use potential fields for local reactive behavior but combine them with global planners or minima-escape strategies for reliable navigation.

A subtle but critical bug in Kalman Filter implementations is incorrect covariance prediction. The exam code example showed P = A * P + Q, which is missing the right multiplication by A transpose. The correct propagation is P = A * P * A' + Q. This term rotates and scales the covariance ellipse according to system dynamics; without it, the covariance loses the correct orientation and size as the state evolves. To test your implementation, use a state transition that rotates the state, such as a constant angular velocity in a 2D pose. Start with a diagonal covariance and observe whether the uncertainty ellipse rotates with the state. If your code lacks A', the ellipse will not rotate and subsequent Kalman gains will be miscomputed, causing either overconfidence or underconfidence in sensor updates. A practical debugging pattern: run a synthetic simulation where A is known and process noise Q is zero; compute the analytic P and compare to the implementation at each step. Misconception check: adding Q does not compensate for the missing A'—it merely inflates uncertainty but does not give it the correct orientation. Key takeaway: always include the full A P A' term and verify with rotation or shear transformations to detect implementation errors.

The provided Euler-to-rotation-matrix code computes Rx, Ry, and Rz and multiplies them as Rx * Ry * Rz. The principal logic error is assuming an implicit rotation convention without documenting the order. Rotation matrices do not commute; the multiplication order determines the actual sequence of rotations and thus the final orientation. The exam answer points out that for the common aerospace Z-Y-X convention (roll-pitch-yaw), the correct composition is R = Rz * Ry * Rx. Another critical issue is gimbal lock: when pitch equals plus or minus ninety degrees, two rotation axes align and the system loses a degree of freedom, producing singular behavior. This is not a code bug per se, but an inherent limitation of Euler angles. The remedy is to switch to quaternion representations for robust orientation handling or to carefully document the rotation convention and guard against singular pitch angles. A concrete example: for theta equal to ninety degrees, Rx and Rz can align making yaw indistinguishable from roll. Misconception check: changing the multiplication order does not merely re-label axes; it fundamentally changes the mapping from Euler parameters to orientation. Key takeaway: always specify rotation order, test edge cases near ±90 degrees, and prefer quaternions when avoiding gimbal lock is required.

Camera intrinsic parameters describe internal camera properties: focal length, principal point, and lens distortion coefficients. These parameters map 3D camera coordinates to pixel coordinates and are essential for accurate projection and triangulation. Bundle adjustment, used in Structure from Motion, refines camera poses and 3D points by minimizing reprojection error across all views; it optimizes poses and point coordinates jointly to produce a maximum likelihood estimate under Gaussian noise assumptions. However, monocular SfM cannot determine absolute scene scale because the essential or fundamental matrix recovers translation only up to a scalar factor. In other words, from a single moving camera you can infer relative geometry but not absolute distances without a scale reference, such as a known object size or stereo baseline. A common practical consequence is that reconstructions from a single camera must be scaled later if metric measurements are required. Misconception check: higher-quality images or better feature matches do not remove the scale ambiguity; only additional metric information or sensors (e. g., stereo baseline, IMU, or known object sizes) resolve scale. Key takeaway: calibrate intrinsics carefully and remember that monocular SfM needs an external scale reference for metric reconstructions.
